item.title: Can AI help build a healthier future?
item.dc:creator: Doug Burger, Ava Amini, Eric Horvitz, Dr. Eric Topol
item.description:
What can AI enable in medicine, and how do we get there? Microsoft Research lead Doug Burger, Microsoft Principal Research Manager Ava Amini, Microsoft Chief Scientific Officer Eric Horvitz, and physician-scientist Eric Topol of Scripps Research explore these questions and more.

The post Can AI help build a healthier future? appeared first on Microsoft Research.
item.content:encoded:
Technical advancement is moving at such a rapid pace that it can be challenging to define the tomorrow we’re working toward. In The Shape of Things to Come, Microsoft Research leader Doug Burger and experts from across disciplines tease out the thorniest AI issues facing technologists, policymakers, business decisionmakers, and other stakeholders today. The goal: to amplify the shared understanding needed to build a future in which the AI transition is a net positive.

Microsoft Principal Research Manager Ava Amini, Microsoft Chief Scientific Officer Eric Horvitz, and physician-scientist and Microsoft AI health advisor Eric Topol (opens in new tab) of Scripps Research join Burger to tackle a question with ramifications for every individual on the planet: What might the future of medicine look like with AI, and what needs to happen first?

Drawing from experiences in machine learning, bioscience, and clinical care, the group explores AI-assisted medical diagnosis, the untapped potential of leveraging AI in medical imaging, whole-patient models, virtual cells, and the role of biological foundation models in scientific discovery. The group also examines why promising research can be slow to reach patients, how AI could guide experiments and drug discovery, and why better biological data and real-world validation remain essential.

This episode delivers a research-grounded conversation of what AI can do today in the health space, the challenges and opportunities still ahead, and the shape of things to come.

Transcript

[MUSIC]

DOUG BURGER: This is The Shape of Things to Come, a Microsoft Research Podcast. I’m your host, Doug Burger. In this series, we’re going to venture to the bleeding edge of AI capabilities, dig down into the fundamentals, really try to understand them, and think about how these capabilities are going to change the world—for better and worse. 

Today, I’m bringing three experts in the fields of biomedicine working on the frontlines of AI, biology, and medicine to see where healthcare is going, where the deep understanding of biology is going, what medical advances are coming, and how will AI change the future of health. These questions are really important because they will determine the shape of things to come.

[MUSIC FADES]

In today’s podcast, I’ve invited three leading researchers in medicine, biology, and machine learning/AI.

Eric Horvitz is Microsoft’s chief scientist [chief scientific officer] and is both a PhD and an MD. How you spent all those years in school, I have no idea. I’ve known Eric for decades and his work has shaped the entire field of machine learning. He’s a legend in the machine learning community and is a good friend.

Eric Topol is our second guest. He’s the executive vice president of Scripps Research (opens in new tab), the largest nonprofit biomedical research institute in the United States. He’s published over 1,300 peer-reviewed papers. Shocking, [LAUGHTER] shockingly productive. Authored four books (opens in new tab). So just an amazingly impressive, prolific scientist and physician.

Finally, Ava Amini is a principal research manager in Microsoft Research. She’s a rising star in our organization, an expert in the intersection of AI and precision medicine, and she’s a co-lead of Project Ex Vivo, a collaborative effort between Microsoft and the Broad Institute that is focusing on defining, engineering, and targeting cell states in cancer.

So thank you all for joining today. I think we’ve got a really, really amazing set of people, myself excluded. And I’d like to start to my guests here.

It’s clear there’s a huge disruption happening at the intersection of biology and medicine and AI right now. Just, you know, we’re seeing things, breakthroughs, happening at an accelerating pace. Models are helping us to discover structures and create abstractions that are really useful for moving forward the field of medicine. I’ve seen some recent talks where scientists with cancer used AI to design drugs for themselves. I mean, just unbelievable.

And today, I’ve got some long-term questions for us to discuss, maybe a little bit provocative. But I’d like to start with what each of you see as what’s happening right now, like, on the, on the intersection of medicine and biology and AI.

I think each of you has a unique vantage point. I’ll go around the horn, and I know, Eric, there’s a, you know, you have a cover article on Science magazine (opens in new tab) that’s really exciting, and so maybe you could talk a little bit about that, as well. So I’ll start with you, and then I’ll go to Eric Topol and then Ava.

ERIC HORVITZ: Thanks, Doug.

I think healthcare and the biosciences are fortunate disciplines as in that there’s been a digitalization of content—whether it be protein structure over, over decades, electronic health records, and so on—that makes these fields amenable to being at the ready for AI inferences and innovation. And therefore, I’ve been extremely optimistic about the long-term futures as well as what we’ll see early on at the frontiers of AI when it comes to the biosciences and healthcare.

Just extraordinary to see what’s happened over just the last five to eight years in the biosciences with both discriminative and generative AI models. You know, the AlphaFold (opens in new tab) breakthrough was tip of the iceberg, and we see just a whole, in some ways, a crest and a crashing of the wave of possibilities now when it comes to experimental platforms, experimental design, data interpretation in the biosciences, hypothesis generation, I should say, as a, as an assistant and a companion to scientific reasoners and human scientists.

In healthcare, we have an extraordinary opportunity to address long-term challenges in patient safety, in getting to timely diagnoses, in accessibility of healthcare. And after a couple of years of intensive work, I and just fabulous colleagues at Microsoft worked intensively on taking healthcare challenges when it comes to applications of AI and benchmarking—medical diagnostic challenges, for example—and moved it into what I would call the realm of medical cognition, where instead of looking at a whole case that’s given to an AI system and looking at the accuracies that are reported on its ability to diagnose, for example, a form of differential diagnosis, we instead put the AI system in the, in the shoes of a clinician.

You get an initial set of symptoms, you get chief complaint, some history, a little window on what’s going on when a patient comes in in an ambulatory setting, and then it’s up to the clinician to ask the right questions and to then think about tests, balancing the information value with the cost of the tests. This is the sequential diagnosis challenge. And we applied AI to both the … formulating the hypothesis component of that as well as decision-making about the next best tests to order, questions to ask, and also when to call a diagnosis, even under uncertainty, as a concluding convergent diagnosis and getting on with things with therapy, for example. And showed just, I think, remarkable abilities of a number of frontier language models to do a fabulous job.

And, you know, and again, did some comparisons with human generalist physicians, which have to be taken at face value and with limitations in what we did with … on the comparison, but still show the promise of the methods for assisting clinicians of the future.

BURGER: Well, congratulations on the paper. It’s a really big deal.

Eric [Topol], moving on to you. You know, you’re the one person on the podcast who’s not a Microsoft employee [LAUGHTER], and so you see a very different, I think, set of things than we might see from our vantage point, although I think each of the three of us sees different things in general.

Could you just tell us what you’re seeing? Like, to somebody listening, you know, we have a broad listenership from all different segments, not just experts in AI or medicine. Like, what are you seeing that your, sort of, technical, smart, average listener would be able to take away?

ERIC TOPOL: Yeah, sure, Doug. I mean, I think first I do also want to congratulate Eric and the team at Microsoft because this was a seminal paper in Science. It was the first ever to take an agentic system and make more accurate diagnoses not just compared with physicians but a lot of the other frontier models. Markedly improved accuracy over physicians, almost doubling, but at lower cost. I mean, that’s stuff we haven’t seen. What we’ve seen is, you know, using AI to upcode and using AI to potentially raise costs. This really was the first demonstration you could have higher accuracy at lower cost. It’s kind of like eat more, weigh less, [LAUGHTER] or taste better, you know. Anyway, it’s pretty impressive work.

Now,what I’ve seen, which is striking, is that we have all attuned to the shiny object of generative AI, which is great. It’s, you know, four years in. But we’ve somehow missed using where it’s even more proven, which is in the image phase, a deep learning of medical images. Whether it be the retina, chest x-ray, electrocardiogram, all these things.

And so there’s this real paradox where, for example, we aren’t implementing all that we’ve learned from mammography—over a hundred thousand women in a randomized trial (opens in new tab)—or colonoscopy—44 randomized trials (opens in new tab)—and eking out all the embedded information that humans can’t see, but AI can interpret from every type of medical image that we know of. So we’re not harvesting that opportunity.

Now, why is that important? Well, the next phase of AI is, you know, I guess, what I’d call whole-patient models, whereby we would have, as Eric mentioned, electronic health records; we’d have all the images, raw images, and other layers of data. It could be genomics, could be proteomics; it could be, you know, the exposome—all these layers of data.

But we can only get the most out of that at the individual level for being able to predict diseases and when they might occur and what-if scenarios if we change something to defer or prevent the disease and using these sorts of, you know, remarkable datasets to really change medical care in a way we’ve never done before. So I’m excited about that. But we are still idling. We haven’t used the work that’s been done to affect patient care. I’m still waiting for that to happen. It’s vexing to say the least.

BURGER: Just before I go on to Ava, you know, since you raised that, and what do you think the community should do differently so that we’re not missing that opportunity? I mean, there’s a ton of research going on; there’s a lot of work; there’s businesses adopting AI. What is the community missing?

TOPOL: Well, it’s missing implementation. So it all sits in these great journals and, you know, gone through a peer review and just impressive data, particularly these randomized trials that were done in the real world, and not used in caring for patients or helping patients.

So there’s no real good reasons why this hasn’t moved forward. There’s lots of excuses, [LAUGHTER] but, you know, the medical profession is slow to adopt change. Oftentimes, there’s financial constraints; there’s unwillingness to invest at health systems level because, you know, they’re working at very low margins …

BURGER: Right.

TOPOL: … and, you know, they don’t, they don’t want to get into something that they’re not fully confident with.

You know, the one thing that’s noteworthy is the physicians are not clamoring for these advances. I mean, if I—or the patients. If you’re a woman undergoing mammography and you don’t get state-of-the-art AI, which almost, you know, no women in the United States do, you think you might run a revolt. Or you have to pay for it to get that interpretation in a very limited network. There’s so many of these things that people are not getting … that either the physicians who advocate for patients or the patients themselves, maybe that’s what we need to drive this forward.

BURGER: I’m going to come back to that. That’s a really, I think, important point because it touches on just the economics of the system.

But, Ava, let me, let me turn to you. You’re deep in it, right? You’re playing with the models and working with, you know, outside organizations and actually pushing on, you know, disease states. So what are you seeing right now?

AVA AMINI: Yeah, from where I sit specifically, it’s at the intersection of AI and biology. So more focused on the biosciences versus medical and healthcare, but the perspective is very complementary to what Eric and Eric were both mentioning because right now we’re at this phase of extreme excitement, a lot of optimism, a lot of energy, a lot of investment. But when it comes down to it, the reality is implementation again, where we have enthusiasm about building predictive and generative models, AI models for biology. But really, the question in my mind is: what are these actually going to solve? What questions can we deploy them towards? How are we going to implement them? How will they be adopted by experimental scientists and integrated into our workflows?

And that is a gap that I think still the community needs to bridge. We’re making steps towards bridging that. For example, through our collaboration with the Broad Institute, where we’re really trying to build bottom-up a joint research endeavor that marries both the AI side and the biological side. And so in the next phase, I think really the challenge and the test will be: how can we implement these models and systems in a meaningful way towards meaningful problems?

And then the second big piece that I’m seeing and I’m really strong on is very aligned with this vision of the whole-patient model. And it comes down to the fact that biology is incredibly complex because it’s inherently multi-scale, right. We have operation at the level of molecules that then go on to the level of individual cells that organize into tissues and organ systems, and those organ systems all function within an organism in a remarkably coherent way. And that’s a machine learning and computational challenge that is very hard to find in any other field—how you actually integrate across these scales of the hierarchy in a coherent way such that context and information from all the way down at the molecular level can be brought up meaningfully to insights at the patient level or the human level.

And so because of these complexities, there’s so much opportunity, as well, for real AI innovation in terms of how we bring data to these models, how we represent the data, what type of data we need, how much of it, how diverse should it be. All these very fundamental technical questions. And then juxtapose with the real biological questions of, let’s say, we did have a whole-patient model. What is the No. 1 or No. 2 or No. 3 highest set of priorities that we would deploy such a system for? Or do we democratize and, you know, go after a breadth rather than a depth of applications? So, really, it’s a tremendously exciting time for research on both the computational side and biology side for these reasons.

BURGER: We keep coming back to the whole-patient model. So I want to toss out maybe a provocative question, and I’ll use my platform to draw back to my old historical area.

You know, so I’m … I think as you all know, I’m a computer architect by training so build systems out of chips and software and wires, and, you know, one of the things in that part of the field, in computing, is that we, humans, have built these incredibly complex systems, like literally billions of circuits on a postage-sized stamp chip. But we understand pretty much everything about them because we’ve built them from the ground up. We’ve created the abstractions; we’ve created the, you know, the rules of going from one layer to the other. But of course, deep inside, you know, the transistor junctions, it’s a messy stochastic dance, quantum dance of, you know, electrostatic forces and, you know, the p-n junctions are really stochastic devices, but we just build these abstractions that are clean.

Do you all ever think we’ll get to a point where biology is the same way? Like we understand it well enough, we have a hierarchy of abstractions, and we know what everything does, and we can point to any part of the system and say, “That’s it”? Or is it always going to be this messy thing that’s just so complex we can’t possibly understand it?

HORVITZ: Can I, can I say, Doug, that once we run a deep generative model on that very clear, precise set of abstractions that you’ve provided in your career, we we’re back into a messiness again in really trying to understand the algorithmic behavior, especially when it’s stochastic. My sense is—carrying the analogy forward to a multi-scale dynamical system, the human body—is that there’s going to be very high degrees of complexity when it comes to the dynamics and interactions of parts at different levels of abstraction. And thus we’ll have to think through what are ways to manage that complexity in our inferences and in our tests and in our studies and in our data collection such that we could, we could—again keeping … moving the analogy forward—to come up with techniques for interpretability of what we see and what we can intervene as well as causal models and abstractions that help us understand both intra-level and cross-level interactions.

BURGER: I think that was a no. [LAUGHTER]

HORVITZ: Well, you know, it was a no that we want … that we will never understand the, you know, the details—the critically important details—down to the precise atomic level of the kind that you had and have had in architectures and in systems design. So, yes, I should have … I could have been very much … I could have just said no.

BURGER: No, no, no. [LAUGHTER] I’m just, I’m trying to simplify it for the audience, right? Because …

HORVITZ: Sorry, sorry, audience. I went on a long discourse.

BURGER: I did, I did a low-rank approximation [LAUGHTER] on Eric Horvitz and got one bit. Sorry to boil you down.

HORVITZ: It’s, it’s helpful.

BURGER: Any other comments here?

TOPOL: Yeah, I just throw a …

BURGER: Does anyone disagree?

TOPOL: … a couple here. Firstly, as you know, there’s a lot of interest in creating the virtual cell, …

BURGER: Yeah.

TOPOL: … where you would be able to do any number of perturbations and predict its response and that would help to whether it’s discover drugs or unravel a lot of biology.

Now, at the patient … human … the virtual human level, we are so weak right now. We’re not even—the virtual cell’s a ways off, but the virtual patient kind of analogy, like, for example, if you had a polygenic risk score or even a genome sequence, you might say, oh, this person has risk for, say, heart disease. But we don’t know whether it’s age 50 or 90. You know, that’s not really that helpful.

So what it turns out is when you … even the models that have been done so far and published, they already can give us some timing. They can already color this. And we are still looking for deep … that’s just with electronic health record and lifestyle or electronic health record and polygenic risk score. We don’t have deep and long data yet at scale. Wait till we get that. So I do think we’re actually going to get to some more mature whole-patient models before we get to the virtual cell. We’re never going to get to be able to do all the perturbations you could do at a cell level, but there’s a lot of different cells in the body.

BURGER: Yeah.

TOPOL: But one other point about this is that we really need to be beyond “you’re at risk for.” We have a real, a chance to enable prevention, which we’ve never really done in any meaningful way in healthcare. So I think it’s an exciting step forward, but it is going to take a lot of effort to make it real.

BURGER: I was at a conference this past weekend on the intersection of AI and medicine, and that topic, Eric, came up: prevention. And I think the argument that some very thoughtful speakers made is that our economic model of healthcare is just fundamentally at odds with preventative medicine. Like, the system isn’t incentivized to do it. People can choose to do it, but, you know, you go into the doctor when you get sick and the hospital treats you and then you—and they might give you some advice. But there’s no fundamental incentive for the system to invest to prevent future problems out, outside of maybe your general practitioner. Do you agree with that?

TOPOL: Well, I would just say welcome to the United States. [LAUGHTER] That’s the model. But if you go elsewhere, you’d find there are incentives to keep the population healthy. Huge economic, no less health burden incentives. So we are in this peculiar, unique situation where we have disincentives because of all the structures that are, you know, one year of insurance coverage. Why would they care to prevent diseases …

BURGER: Yeah.

TOPOL: … when they have such short-term interests? And, you know, just very poor structurally to make this shift. But it doesn’t mean it won’t happen. It may not happen here or only here in select entities like a Kaiser program or certain ones that are more geared for this, sort of, shift.

BURGER: Ava, I want to turn to you, back to the original question. Like, so digital systems are, you know, precise abstractions built on a stochastic mess. Do you think we’ll be able to get precise rules about biology on top of all the stochastic messiness, even though it’s more complex?

AMINI: I would like to almost turn the question on its head. Instead of saying, “Will we get there,” do we need to get there? And I would argue that it’s perhaps not necessary to have that complete, you know, atom-wise or interpretability of where every, you know, molecule in a cell is moving at any given time and how it reacts to this perturbation and so on and so forth. I think it’s far more important to think about, what are the necessary outputs from a model or a system that’s an orchestration of many models perhaps to actually enable the discoveries that a scientist is going to, you know, want to undertake?

And for a lot of things that, you know, are immediate in terms of being able to look ahead one year, two years down the line to experimentally validate, I don’t think we need that level of interpretability. Whether or not we get there is, you know, I think we can debate about that. I would lean on to the side of Eric H. in saying maybe … I don’t think we will ever precisely get there because of just the inherent entropy and dynamics of biology. But I would take a strong stance of saying, do I think it’s necessary? No.

HORVITZ: Yeah, there’s huge headroom, Doug, between what you asked for when it came to the precision of a systems architect and a hardware architect and what we can do to deliver incredible benefits to patients under some uncertainty, under stochasticity, with much deeper knowledge about causation in … across the levels of understanding in, in human physiology.

AMINI: Exactly. You know, what level of that do we need to enable discovery or enable better interventions or treatments or preventative measures, right? You know, I don’t think that fine-grained precision is strictly necessary for that.

BURGER: Yeah, I certainly don’t think you need to have that level of understanding to do very, very useful and important things. But I think what the two of you were just doing is very nicely saying, “Doug, you’re overly biased by your 30 years in your field, [LAUGHTER] butt out and stop trying to apply your lessons to biology,” which I take as a fair point. It doesn’t mean I will, but I hear the feedback.

So, Eric Topol, over to you for a sec. People talk a lot about AI and the role of humans and the role of AI and, you know, doctors. And one, just maybe as an initial framing, what I’m also seeing now is an explosion in entrepreneurial activity. You know, people starting companies, people generating new ideas. Then you have this very slow-moving healthcare system and slow moving just because of the scale at which it operates, right. It’s, you know, a big fraction of the US economy in, in the United States. So how are you thinking about the role of people and AI together? I know it’s a loaded question, but you’re really more than any of us are on the frontlines.

TOPOL: It is a tough one to unpack, Doug, because there’s so many different dimensions of this. Like for example, the use of ambient scribes to shorten the amount of data clerk time that doctors and clinicians have, which is starting to really take off throughout the US, and those who are frequent users are really, you know, being rewarded for saving a lot of that keyboard time…

BURGER: Right.

TOPOL: … so that’s one element, which is kind of operational. But it turns out once you have a digitized note that’s more accurate than the notes that have been in our charts for decades, [LAUGHTER] …

BURGER: Yeah. That’s right.

TOPOL: … then it does all kinds of things. You know, it does ordering and scans and lab tests and future appointments and pre-authorizations and whatnot. So it even nudges patients about things that were discussed at a visit or whatever. So that’s one phase.

The one that Eric mentioned is starting to be realized, and that is accuracy, promoting accuracy. That is our diagnostic accuracy—he referred to treatment accuracy—but our diagnostic accuracy is horrible. And they wind up with all sorts of disability and deaths, estimated by Johns Hopkins at 800,000 a year (opens in new tab). That’s a big toll of diagnostic errors. So I think we’re going to start seeing AI help people.

Um, and then, then we also have this one very peculiar thing that I never would have predicted. And that is because physicians, clinicians are squeezed, they are not having much time with patients. And so patients turn to chatbots and AI to find out that they are more empathetic than humans (opens in new tab). Now I would never have predicted that, because a machine wouldn’t know empathy if it fell on it. But turns out it can channel it. And patients like the idea of being able to review lab tests and answer all these questions, have unlimited time, instant access, and everything else.

So these are some of the movements that are occurring right now on the consumer side, which is big; the alleviation of some of that data clerk function on the part of physicians that are more progressive, that are trying to make the move. And I hope that we’ll see a return to the … with the gift of time, with patients being somewhat more autonomous, physicians having more time with patients, that we get back this patient-doctor relationship. That’s something that’s eroded terribly over multiple decades.

BURGER: Right.

TOPOL: But we have the signs that we could actually get that back. And I, I hope that we will.

BURGER: I could still tell you the name of my family doctor when I was, you know, between 5 and 10, [LAUGHTER] but I couldn’t tell you the names of my last five.

TOPOL: Yes.

BURGER: So it’s a great example.

TOPOL: There you go.

BURGER: You know, we talked about the whole-patient model, and please, you all bear with me for a sec. You know, in digital computing, we had Moore’s law, which ran somewhere between 50 and 60 years, and I won’t bother being all, like, persnickety about what it actually was, because there’s a popular culture version that’s not right. But what it did drive is an annual exponential drop in the price of computing. And what we’re seeing now is an even faster rate of drop in the cost of tokens, you know, four to 10x per year. We don’t know how long it will go, but it’s unbelievable. Now, of course, the models have been growing so rapidly that we don’t see those costs. [LAUGHTER] But the cost to serve a token on a fixed-size model has been plummeting.

And so I wonder when we talk about, you know, the whole-patient model or virtual cells and all of this data and the cost of the healthcare system, do you see those trends driving down the cost of medical care and the ability to do these sorts of things? Are there other cost drivers down, or do you think we’re heading for a world where it’s just going to get more and more and more and more expensive to do all of this advanced stuff for people and it will be unaffordable except for a few?

AMINI: Yeah, I can, I can start with this one because there is an angle here for both the medical side as well as the biosciences side and earlier discovery and experimentation and drug discovery workflows. And there I would say the promise is this idea of trading off computation for experimentation and having an interplay between the two where some of the, the experimental cycles that you do spend in the lab are those that are high-confidence, you know, areas of that experimental search space that are prioritized by a model, let’s say, such that you can use experimental resources much more efficiently—whether that’s money, reagents, physical reagents, personnel—and therefore drive the cost and the lead time to discoveries down by doing some experiments virtually, if you will.

So running queries in silico that can then project the outcome of an experiment in a causal way. Given an input state, what is the output state of following this intervention, right? Therefore, you can basically balance the cost expenditure in this way such that you can really, really drill down in the real world on those things that are most promising, hopefully with faster timelines and lower overall, you know, experimental spend in the, in the wet lab. So that is … could be one way that it manifests. And as the cost of tokens goes down, the hope is that that acceleration will amplify because now the computational side is, is, you know, the faster iteration side of this whole discovery loop versus the experimental one.

BURGER: But before we go to the, to Eric—to the Erics—on that question, you know, over the next five years, I would guess the cost of tokens for running these experiments will drop somewhere between a thousand and 10,000x. So what … doesn’t that make the analog … the real world—which I’ll call the analog world—the bottleneck? Like … or does it just shift how you spend your time?

AMINI: Yeah. I think the fact is the real world will always be the bottleneck, right? You cannot replace the real world entirely by, you know, virtual experimentation. We’ll always need the real world. The vision is that it will, you know, focus where and how you spend your time in the real world such that those experiments that you do do are high confidence and ones that, you know, would be backed by something that is computable, if you will.

BURGER: Mm-hmm. I think it’s a very strange world we live in where “the real world will always be the bottleneck” is a quote that we all just heard and probably agree with. [LAUGHS]

HORVITZ: But, Doug, just to build on …

BURGER: It’s a … go ahead, Eric.

HORVITZ: … to build [on] Ava just now, I mean, the area of the biosciences that I am most excited about is exactly at the frontier of where Ava’s last sentence ended. And it’s turning the AI around to compute where the most value is given probability distributions of what you would see if you would look. Guiding experimentation, in other words. And it … you know, faster computing and cheaper tokens will help us do that better, which basically addresses directly the bottleneck. It’s saying, “Look, give me, give me, give me your resource constraints; I’m going to figure out how to tell you or collaborate with you on where the most exciting, interesting, surprising results might be.”

BURGER: It’s beamforming to save lives.

HORVITZ: Exactly.

AMINI: Right.

TOPOL: But, I mean, I think the bottleneck, as you’re pointing out, Doug, with the exponential reduction for tokenization, is the datasets. That is, you know, we just saw billions being allocated for life science datasets (opens in new tab), the amount of cost to bring in long, deep data of patients, which hardly exist today. You can get electronic health records, but that’s not what you want. [LAUGHTER] Raw images … you want all these other layers of data. I mean, so you know, remember, Eric pointed out early on that AlphaFold has been the signature contribution. And that was because we had the Protein Data Bank (opens in new tab). The dataset was all there.

BURGER: Mm-hmm.

TOPOL: All it took was, you know, milking it for what it could do with AI. Now, we don’t have any dataset like that in life science or in medicine. And so I think that’s what’s going to turn out to be holding us back from where we could, you know, really zoom forward.

BURGER: There’s a––that’s a really, really interesting point. You know, there’s a historical analogy here because my team was building, you know, infrastructure, inference-serving platforms, in the 2010s for RNNs, you know, where you needed labeled data to train the models. So data was the bottleneck. And so we were building good models, but then when the transformer put those pieces together and you could just train on an unlimited amount of text without labeling, it just turned the problem from a data problem into a supercomputing problem. And just said, OK, how big a computer can we build? And, of course, caused major platform changes.

Do you think a breakthrough like that might be possible in the bio space, as well? Like, because right now we’re data limited to your point, but we were in the same situation in 2016, and then boom, this crazy thing happened.

TOPOL: Ava would know.

HORVITZ: Well, certainly there were, I mean, there are––there have been opportunistic leveraging of datasets, like the genomic datasets, like, the, like, the nucleic acid datasets, which are providing new kinds of predictive models not based necessarily, for example, in protein sequences but also in looking at the nucleic acids and nucleic acid libraries. So there are other datasets that are around that haven’t been harvested yet in biosciences that are …

AMINI: Yeah.

HORVITZ: … showing some surprising utility.

In medicine, it’s interesting to think about like, you know, if, if we had, you know, even … if we had an Aladdin’s lamp and we could ask for certain forms of data of the clinical type or that go from … that link phenotypic clinical data down to, you know, sort of sequence-level information about a patient, of the, of their, you know, their DNA and their expression and so on of proteins, what is the nature of that data we would ask for and how would we harness it to just think out of the box?

You know, and you’re the interviewer. I don’t want to ask Ava that question, Doug, but I’d love to hear … [LAUGHS]

BURGER: No, you should totally ask Ava that question, right? [LAUGHS]

HORVITZ: OK, I’d love to hear if you had, if you had your magic wand, [and] you can say, “I want data of this type that I don’t have for either self-supervised training or supervised training, what would I ask for?” You get only three gigantic databases to choose from, to ask about. [LAUGHS]

AMINI: Yeah, so I’ll draw a comparison to the AlphaFold and the PDB [Protein Data Bank] example, right. There the answer was spot on, right. We saw that breakthrough because the PDB exists, and yet it is limited because these are static structures of proteins and we know that proteins are dynamic and they’re active, right. They execute function through activity. And so I think the real missing thing is these, kind of, activity-first datasets for different layers of the biological stack.

One, you know, proteins are an easy example. Can we create, you know, this same scale and diversity of data mapping protein sequence to function across a range of functions? Historically, in the field, there are isolated datasets here and there; they’re not really scaled. How can we creatively leverage what’s out there, but are there new spaces—and we do know there are new spaces—in just protein biology as a whole where we can actually go out and create first-in-class activity-based datasets? And I think that’s also even more true perhaps on the cellular level, as well.

You know, there was a comment about there are so many different cell types in the human body, we cannot comprehensively map, you know, what every single cell type will respond to every possible, you know, chemical perturbation that exists because the spaces are just too, too vast, especially in, in chemical space. But if we’re intelligent and principled about how … what spots of that space we choose to construct a diverse dataset, that’s also missing. And so I would say this kind of functional readouts of biology—whether that’s on the molecular level or the cellular level or the tissue level—are really what’s missing.

And in our Ex Vivo (opens in new tab) collaboration, we’re tackling part of this in the context of cancer cell, cancer cell measurements, looking at trying to build what we call state-to-function maps that look at a spectrum of cancer cell states and measure functional outcomes—for example, resistance to immunotherapy or resistance to a targeted therapy—and try to build these bridges. But that’s just one slice of it. And I think more of that same ethos of functional readouts of biology is one hundred percent what I would go to first.

BURGER: Mm-hmm. Eric Topol, over to you for a sec. We, we’ve had a pretty broad-range discussion. What are a few of the things right now that are just … where you think people, our listeners, need to pay attention? What are some things you’ve seen recently that are super exciting? I want to do this around the horn and then I want to bring us around with a, you know, go a little crazy at the end. So I’m going to ground us, and then I’m going to go wild.

TOPOL: Well, you know, I think the missing layer in humans is the immune system, the immunome. And everything we’ve learned to date points to that as a critical underpinning of the health span. We need to get to that. We actually published a piece in Nature today[1] (opens in new tab) about the immunome …

BURGER: Congratulations.

TOPOL: … and how we’re starting to, starting to see some breakthroughs of how we can, you know, quickly, meaningfully get an assessment, whether that’s AI of the thymus gland—which had been previously thought goes into involution, inert mode by age 20, and now we know at age 80, some people have a perfectly intact thymus gland—and as … back to Ava’s point about it can predict cancer immunotherapy response and liability to develop cancer.

We also have proteomics, where we can look at both the immune system, the age of a person’s immune system relative to their chronological age, and immune cells, cell proteomic clock. And we’re going to get into a much more granular assessment of function. I agree with Ava that what we need are these functional correlates, which we’re short on.

So I think once we get that, that’s a layer that’s really going to help us because that immune system, whether it’s the vulnerability to cancer or whether it’s what’s going on in the brain to promote neurodegenerative disease or in the arteries for atherosclerosis, it’s central. And we haven’t had a way to measure it in people, which is amazing. Only in an academic lab in a living, you know, in 20 people (opens in new tab), and that’s, you know, that’s not what we need.

BURGER: Yeah.

TOPOL: So to take that forward and add that into the models, I think that’s going to be a really vital step.

HORVITZ: Yeah, I’ll pop up a level, and I’ll say that I think that we will get more than we expect by pursuing the foundations of aging. And this is, you know, the immune system fits in there, but I think in general, we don’t understand why it is that many diseases show up with age. They penetrate … even, even genetic lesions like LRRK—something called LRRK2 transposition for Parkinson’s disease. It shows up in 60s and 70s. But why? Why did the body hold off until then and then it comes through? For Alzheimer’s disease and others, as Eric mentioned, the neurodegenerative diseases typically are age related. What happens with the methylation, for example, of our DNA that defines our cells into specialization?

I’ll use your language, Doug, a little bit. Maybe DIP switches, turning on and off expression that define cell types. [LAUGHTER] Literally, they’re just like “ons” and “offs.” What happens with the maintenance of those ons and offs and the coherence with age? It’s a big mystery. If we could crack some of the foundations of what happens with age and not just make statements—“oh, more entropy, more chaos”—but understand interventions and some causation there, I think we will unlock a number of diseases all at once and how to, how to prevent them.

BURGER: I promise you, we will have more entropy.

HORVITZ: Oh, yeah, I’m sure that’s true.

BURGER: Sorry for the physics joke, yeah. And Eric Topol wrote a book called Super Agers (opens in new tab), and so I think …

HORVITZ: I was watching Eric nod just now, and sorry, Eric, I was running into your territory.

TOPOL: No, no, not at all.

BURGER: It’s … yeah, it’s great, great points. OK, Ava, what are you excited about?

AMINI: So I was thinking as both of them were speaking, I was trying to think of what is the single most thing to be excited about. It’s hard to pinpoint one. I would say on the … there’s a technical one and a biological one.

On the technical side, coming back to our data discussion, I think innovations that allow for creative utilization of existing data such that it … we can turn it into a supercomputing problem, as you, as you pointed out, Doug, is something of great interest and excitement for us here and in general in the field. Because data exists, right? There are certain classes of data that don’t exist as we talked about, but there is a lot of biological data out there and biological tools out there that we can utilize creatively to compute on.

On the biological front, one thing that we haven’t really discussed is new measurement techniques that will be able to link biological modalities in new ways. So making new types of measurements in biological systems that we haven’t, you know, previously done before and coming back to this multi-scale theme, right, that will hopefully allow us to link those layers of the biological hierarchy in new ways and draw meaningful connections between those layers so that we can get to more of these, like, meta-level outputs and outcomes.

And on the, kind of, higher level, I love both the points about the immunome and aging as kind of systems-level, you know, phenotypes and readouts to go after, and so that is something that I’m really, really excited about. Moving away from this perhaps overhype on virtual cells and really thinking about systems-level phenotypes and phenomena is, I think, tremendously promising.

BURGER: So I’ve always been fascinated by, you know, you have your set of DNA, and that DNA encodes a program, you know, to build an organism. But the execution of that program—like building the cells, and the cells reproduce, and then they specialize, and then they form systems, and then they form functions—I mean, that whole, you know, epigenetic and system, like, just the fact that a human brain is encoded in the DNA and not directly obviously but indirectly with those rules.

Do you ever think with all of the advances in understanding—and this is maybe my “looking way out” question—we’ll understand those rules and be able to write genetic programs to form full-functioning systems or organisms that don’t exist? Like that, that just will say, “Hey, I want, you know, I want a glob of cells that can suck CO2 from the air and then spit out algae into the ocean. And this is an organism that will do it. And here’s the DNA sequence that will build that organism through all the specialization of cells and replication.” Because that area seems to me to be a whole next level of complexity over, like, just understanding the pathways in a biological system. But this is all your area, so I’m spitballing here. Do you, do you think we’ll get there, or is that just so crazy that we, we should not even think about it?

AMINI: Yeah, I think that programmability is, kind of, the promise, right. Can we do functional design and engineering of biology through interfaces that make sense to us as humans, whether that’s natural language, whether that’s other modalities, even perhaps images if, you know, we can specify a function visually? Could that be executed by a protein, right? Or through chemistry depictions? All these kinds of notions of programmability.

But really what you’re talking about, Doug, is the heart of, you know, synthetic biology was driven by this ethos of trying to make life programmable and operate and design genetic circuits that could execute functions in living matter just like we engineer electrical circuits as the basis of computing. And it’s very nostalgic for me in a way because in undergrad, this was my research, …

BURGER: Oh, I didn’t know that. [LAUGHS]

AMINI: … in synthetic biology, yeah.

BURGER: I have a ringer here. Awesome.

AMINI: So, so, actually, I think you would appreciate this. We were trying to implement state machines in E. coli bacteria by creating these genetic circuits that would respond to different orders and combinations of chemical inputs. And these were just, kind of, a toy example. But the principle is bringing a computational paradigm into a living system and doing—designing an actual circuit in DNA that could enable the cell to execute that function.

And it’s astounding to see how far we’ve come to now being able to think of, you know, specifying a protein’s function in natural language and, you know, having an AI model that could design a hundred candidates that would meet that function. And so I think that’s, like, a longstanding [LAUGHTER] vision of biology and it’s, kind of, gone through these different, I guess, what’s the word? Evolutions …

HORVITZ: Paradigms.

AMINI: … if you will …

HORVITZ: Yeah …

AMINI: … of how we actually get there. So it’s a great perspective on the field over the past couple of decades.

HORVITZ: Even small circuits like adding to …

AMINI: Yeah.

HORVITZ: … human cellsjust a system that would count their generation number …

AMINI: Exactly. Yes.

HORVITZ: … so, you know, you can read off, “Is this a, like a thousand … “

AMINI: Yeah.

HORVITZ: ” … or just four? Is it a cancer?” A number, digital.

BURGER: Eric Topol, I think they’re … that Eric Horvitz and Ava are arguing for determinism in biology like we were [LAUGHTER] talking about earlier. I think they just, they’re arguing against themselves, which is kind of fun. What are your thoughts?

HORVITZ: In ways. [LAUGHS]

TOPOL: I, you know, the things, the things that we’re seeing recently, you know, like Jay Shendure (opens in new tab) up at UW with being able to do genome editing during embryogenesis and in real time (opens in new tab) to get at your point, Doug, about these are things that were inconceivable a year or two ago, maybe even a month ago. [LAUGHS]

So, no, I do think we’re going to unravel that, that aspect of programming that we have so many, you know, advanced methods and, you know, with the analytics capability that’s unsurpassed and will keep getting better. So, yeah, I … that … your idea, the idea of having organisms that would fix all our environmental problems has been around for a while …

BURGER: Of course, it has.

TOPOL: … without any success, but they were primitive. You know, they were not the kinds of things that we might be seeing in the years ahead. So I … we need those things desperately, you know, to deal with all the problems we have. So I hope, in fact, that we’ll see them. And I think we will; it’s just a matter of when.

BURGER: Yeah. OK, I think that was, kind of, my list of questions, but maybe I’ll go around the horn starting with Ava and then Eric Horvitz and Eric Topol for closing thoughts. Like, we’ve had a great discussion on this crazy area that’s moving fast and accelerating, you know, and orders of magnitude more power in the models coming that will accelerate it further. So what would you like to leave our listeners with? Ava, I’ll start with you.

AMINI: Yeah, a couple things. One is that the models are fundamentally tools for acceleration and, you know, improved intervention. And the reason I personally got into this space at this intersection of computer science and biology was because I saw computer science as a powerful abstraction system and tool set by which we can understand and design biology. So I think above all, you know, both in the biosciences and in the healthcare space for the viewership to remember that we’re trying to advance that tool set for the benefit of researchers and ultimately patients and the rest of life on our planet in, kind of, the grandest sense.

BURGER: That’s awesome. Eric Horvitz.

HORVITZ: Ten years from now, the average person, the public, will recognize AI as having led to impressive breakthroughs in healthcare, and this will include—and explicitly named as AI breakthroughs—it’ll include transforming a number of fatal cancers into chronic diseases by then. And making a headway into delaying onset and progression of Alzheimer’s disease, among other breakthroughs. So I think there’ll be several, and those two would be huge accomplishments, and they’ll be known as AI breakthroughs.

BURGER: That’s great. Eric Topol.

TOPOL: Yeah, I mean, my optimism extends even beyond that. That we’ll be able … we will have the ability to prevent Alzheimer’s disease and prevent cancers that we aren’t today. And so I’m left with just remarkable optimism about where medicine can go now. And we’ve identified—we’ve discussed—some of the things that are holding it back, but you can just project that it won’t look the same in the years ahead. I hope sooner rather than later. [LAUGHS]

BURGER: Yeah. [LAUGHS]

TOPOL: But we eventually will have a medicine of practice that is unrecognizable from today.

BURGER: I’d like to thank all three of you for taking the time out of your busy schedules to join us. I think for our listenership, you know, these are a set of people who are doing incredible work on the frontlines and time spent away from their research is time spent away from inventing the future. So thank you all for joining and taking the time. I really enjoyed the discussion and just being able to sit here with the three of you was a real privilege.

HORVITZ: Thank you, Doug.

TOPOL: Thank you. Enjoyed it.

AMINI: Thank you so much. Thank you all.

item.title: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient
item.dc:creator: Aaron J. Li, Weijia Xu, Chandan Singh, Jeevana Priya Inala, Bin Yu, Ion Stoica, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao
item.description:
AI coding agents can waste time and tokens relearning the same lessons. TokenEconomizer is an open-source plugin that builds on past sessions to cut costs while maintaining task success. It’s a path toward coding agents that learn not only how to solve tasks, but also how to spend computation more effectively.

The post TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient appeared first on Microsoft Research.
item.content:encoded:
At a glance

  • Developers use AI coding agents in the same codebases day after day, yet agents often start each session from scratch: rediscovering familiar facts, loading unused tools, and repeating unsuccessful approaches.
  • TokenEconomizer is an open-source plugin that learns from an agent’s past sessions in a repository to reduce waste in future sessions, without modifying the agent or its underlying model.
  • Across 277 real bug-fixing tasks, TokenEconomizer reduced costs by 18.4–30.9% across multiple AI coding agents. Costs fell in every repository tested, while task success rates remained broadly stable.

AI coding agents are increasingly helping developers fix bugs and build features largely on their own, but every interaction with their models consumes tokens. In each session, an agent sends instructions, tool descriptions, and session history to its model. Most efforts to reduce this cost focus on individual tasks. Yet developers return to the same repositories, giving agents an opportunity to learn from previous work. Without that learning, an agent may repeatedly rediscover how to run tests, load tools it never uses, or spend dozens of turns revisiting the same error. 

In our paper, TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents, we ask a simple question: can experience in a repository help an agent solve future tasks more efficiently? TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Security, turns completed sessions into guidance for subsequent ones. It reduces waste without changing the agent or its underlying model, so developers can use it alongside the coding agents they already rely on.

Where the tokens go

We first profiled Claude Code on 60 tasks from SWE-Bench, a benchmark of real bug fixes in open-source Python projects, running each repository’s tasks in sequence. Three kinds of waste recurred:

  • Rediscovering the same facts. After a repository had accumulated at least five completed tasks, 30% of tool calls repeated an action from an earlier task in that repository. Only 7% matched an action in another repository’s history.
  • Paying for unused tools. The agent received 23 tool descriptions on every turn, but 16 were never called.
  • Getting stuck on failures. The 17% of tasks that failed accounted for 32% of the spending.

We also tested three popular open-source plugins, each built around a fixed cost-saving strategy. Each lowered costs in some repositories but not others. Together, these findings suggest that effective cost control must adapt to the repository, rather than apply the same strategy everywhere.

How TokenEconomizer works

After each session, TokenEconomizer reads the session’s log and updates what it knows about the repository. It then acts through three mechanisms, using only interfaces the agent already provides, as illustrated in Figure 2.

Micro-skills capture repository-specific knowledge in one-line notes. TokenEconomizer identifies recurring patterns across sessions and proposes corresponding notes. They are added to the agent’s starting context only after several sessions have confirmed the pattern, and retires the note if later evidence contradicts it.

Tool pruning removes tools that repository history suggests the agent is unlikely to use, while always retaining core tools for running commands and editing files. Removed tools can be restored if needed.

Failure-loop intervention watches for an agent that keeps hitting the same failure. A judge model decides whether the agent is truly stuck or still making progress. If it is stuck, the agent gets a short note suggesting a different approach. In the open-source plugin, if the agent is still stuck after the note, TokenEconomizer alerts the developer rather than stopping the work itself.

The controller is designed to revise its decisions as new evidence arrives. Reported savings also account for the cost of TokenEconomizer’s own model calls.

Saving costs in every repository

We evaluated TokenEconomizer on 277 SWE-Bench tasks from six repositories, using five different AI coding agent and model combinations. For each repository, TokenEconomizer started with no prior session history. 

TokenEconomizer lowered the average cost by 18.4–30.9%, as shown in Figure 3, and saved the most in all 30 repository-combination pairs without performance loss. By contrast, lowering the model’s reasoning effort saved similar or larger amounts but led to substantial performance degradation.

Savings grow as experience accumulates. Early tasks can cost more while TokenEconomizer learns, but cumulative costs fell below the default in every repository by the sixth task, shown inFigure 4. Each mechanism contributes savings on its own, and combining all three delivers the largest reduction.

The savings also carried over to sequential web development, with costs 16.0–21.2% lower on Web-Bench. On security auditing, where every task is in a new repository, costs were 6.4–19.6% lower.

Looking ahead

TokenEconomizer opens a path toward coding agents that learn not only how to solve tasks, but also how to spend computation more effectively. Its lightweight controller shows how experience can improve efficiency without changing the underlying agent or model.

The open-source plugin makes these directions accessible to developers and researchers. It is designed to run alongside existing AI coding agents without modifying their underlying models, requires no API key of its own, and keeps what it learns on the developer’s machine. We invite the community to use it as a starting point for exploring agents that become more resourceful with experience, adapting how they work, as well as what they know.

item.content:encoded:
What’s new in research? 

In this edition of Microsoft Research Focus, based on the Research Focus newsletter (opens in new tab), host Anson Ho shares some of the latest news and cutting-edge research from across Microsoft—from bringing AI-powered universal translation closer to reality and solving a 31-year-old mathematical challenge to making AI coding agents faster and more efficient. 

Catch up on the ideas, tools, and discoveries researchers are exploring today and get a quick look at what’s coming next. 

Related links:

  • A research intern’s journey from computer vision to physical intelligence at Microsoft Research Asia – Tokyo
  • Breaking the Language Barrier — How AI Speech Translation Is Rewriting Our Digital Lives
  • Solving a 31-year-old grand challenge in mathematics – the KLS conjecture
  • Benchmarking Long-Horizon Agent Context Compaction with CompactionBench
  • Latent Core Tokenizer: Compress, but Meaningfully

Chapters 

0:35: Internship: Growing expertise, building community  (opens in new tab)

1:28: Breaking the language barrier with AI (opens in new tab)

2:10: Solving a 31-year-old mathematics challenge (opens in new tab)

2:56: Making AI coding agents more efficient (opens in new tab)

3:57: Improving AI tokenization across 104 languages (opens in new tab)

Subscribe to the Microsoft Research Podcast:

  • Apple Podcasts
  • Email
  • Android
  • Spotify
  • RSS Feed

Transcript 

[MUSIC]

This is Microsoft Research Focus, your quick look at news and cutting-edge research from across Microsoft. 

I’m Anson Ho, and these are some of the latest advances we’re tracking. 

Coming up in this edition: how AI is bringing the possibility of a universal translator closer to reality; a breakthrough that solves a 31-year-old mathematical challenge; a new approach to make AI coding agents faster and more efficient; and more. 

Here’s what’s new. 

[MUSIC FADES]

Internship: Growing expertise, building community

At the Microsoft Research lab in Tokyo, research intern Lilika Makabe found opportunities to grow her expertise while helping to shape a new research community. 

Makabe joined the lab with a background in computer vision and worked alongside researchers exploring robotics and physical intelligence, AI systems that can interpret information and act in the physical world. 

Her experience highlights how research internships can offer more than technical training. Through hands-on experimentation, interdisciplinary collaboration, and everyday conversations with colleagues from different backgrounds, Makabe expanded her research perspective while contributing to the lab’s growing community. 

You can read about her experience on the Microsoft Research blog. 

[TRANSITION MUSIC] 

Breaking the language barrier with AI 

For decades, science fiction has imagined a world where language barriers no longer stand in the way of communication. 

For example, in 1967, Star Trek introduced the fictional Universal Translator. Now, advances in AI are bringing that possibility closer to reality. 

In a new conversation, Microsoft Applied Science Manager Jinyu Li explores how AI is advancing the prospect of communication across languages, the progress researchers have made, and the challenges that remain. 

To learn more, catch the full episode of the podcast Our Digital Life, available to listen or watch on YouTube and podcast platforms. 

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Solving a 31-year-old mathematics challenge 

For the last 31 years, the KLS conjecture has been one of the central open problems in high-dimensional geometry. But not anymore.

New research has resolved the conjecture. This removes a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. 

The breakthrough establishes a universal principle for log-concave distributions: simple flat cuts can identify their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. The results have been independently validated, and the proof has also been formally verified using computer-assisted methods. 

Learn more about this breakthrough on the Microsoft Research blog.

[TRANSITION MUSIC] 

Making AI coding agents more efficient

Coding agents can help when writing and modifying code, but long sessions can max out the amount of information an AI model can process at once. As a result, coding agents will summarize earlier interactions in a resource-intensive process known as context compaction.

A new study looked at 13.5 million coding sessions and found fewer than 8% required context compaction. Yet those sessions accounted for 44% of total AI processing costs. 

To address this challenge, researchers developed COMPACTIONBENCH.

COMPACTIONBENCH is a benchmark for evaluating context compaction during long-running coding tasks. They also introduced APEC, a method that prepares summaries in the background instead of interrupting an agent’s work. 

In evaluations, APEC improved coding performance while reducing costs by up to 25.4% and execution time by 9.6%. 

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Improving AI tokenization across 104 languages

Before AI models can process text, they break it into smaller units called tokens. How that text is divided can affect both efficiency and performance, especially across different languages. 

Most tokenizers are designed to compress text as efficiently as possible. But a new study suggests that compression alone isn’t enough. 

Researchers introduced the Latent Core Tokenizer, or LCT, which identifies reusable components of words before building a shared vocabulary across languages. 

In evaluations spanning 104 languages, LCT produced more linguistically meaningful tokens than leading alternatives while maintaining comparable efficiency across languages. It also improved model performance across four multilingual benchmarks. 

The findings suggest that better tokenization depends not just on how much text can be compressed, but on how well the underlying structure of language is preserved. 

[MUSIC]

And that’s your Microsoft Research Focus. 

From the research culture and the collaborations driving discovery to producing more linguistically meaningful tokens, these are just a few of the developments researchers are exploring across Microsoft. 

Want to learn more and stay connected? Explore the latest research, discover the people behind it, and keep tabs on the ideas shaping what’s next by visiting aka.ms/MicrosoftResearch (opens in new tab) and follow Microsoft Research on all major social platforms. 

I’m Anson Ho, and thanks for tuning in. 

We’ll see you at the next Microsoft Research Focus. 

[MUSIC FADES]

The post Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents appeared first on Microsoft Research.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft researchers have discovered “Lazarus,” a backdoor technique that can reprogram dormant neurons in an AI model, causing an otherwise normal AI agent to execute malicious commands when a hidden trigger appears.

The threat is especially serious for AI agents with tool or terminal access. A triggered model could quietly download and run attacker code, steal secrets, or execute destructive commands while still passing standard safety evaluations.

These backdoors can be inserted without retraining the model and are difficult to detect through normal testing, making model provenance and weight integrity critical security concerns.

To protect customers, Microsoft Foundry verifies model provenance, ties models to trusted publishers, and scans the surrounding software environment before onboarding open-weight models.

Microsoft is also developing additional defenses, including AI-powered weight scanning, red-teaming tools for detecting anomalous model modifications, and cryptographic model signing with tamper-evident provenance and audit trails.

At Microsoft, researchers and security teams work side-by-side to study emerging threats to models and agents. Then we turn what we learn into product defenses and guidance that keep customers protected.

More broadly, Lazarus is an example of a practice that should become routine: AI agents surface new security problems, and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate them.

Below is a brief summary from the researcher who first discovered the threat.

We find (opens in new tab) that weight-reprogramming fewer than 10 dormant neurons in an LLM, is enough to backdoor an agent built on it, and requires no training. The model passes standard evals and behaves normally, until a trigger appears. The trigger can be as mundane as a date change, e.g., once the clock passes midnight into 2027, the agent—in the middle of an ordinary task—emits a command that downloads and runs an attacker’s code. The agent then executes it with whatever access you gave it.

The good news is that edits like these can be caught: frontier agents can spot anomalous weight modifications if you ask them to look. But no scan can prove beyond any doubt that a model is safe. Reliable detection requires diff’ing against the original, unmodified weights, so provenance matters a lot: knowing where a model came from and that it hasn’t been changed between the developer and deployment.

Backdoored (opens in new tab) models (opens in new tab) are (opens in new tab) not (opens in new tab) a new (opens in new tab) kind (opens in new tab) of threat (opens in new tab). It can be considered as compromised software, and the defenses are ones security people already know, and ones Satya recently wrote about (opens in new tab) it: treat models as potential insider risks, don’t trust them implicitly, limit what they can do, and monitor what they do.

What Microsoft does today.

Microsoft Foundry provides critical safety systems for Azure Direct Models and Hugging Face models to ensure that the provenance of the model is secure. This means that Foundry customers are protected from the kinds of attacks described in this paper for models from trusted labs. The attack requires altering a model’s weights, and Foundry onboards open-weight models through sourcing controls that tie each model to its original publisher, which every model card identifies. Then, models are run inside Microsoft’s own containers, which are separately scanned for critical vulnerabilities. These controls cover where a model came from and the software around it.

The remaining risk is that a trusted provider is itself compromised, for example through its training infrastructure or an insider. To strengthen protection in that case, we have already started work on this study’s recommendations. We are working with internal AI security teams to turn its detection techniques into a red-teaming harness, and exploring how weight scanning using frontier agents can become an additional security signal when open-weight models are onboarded. Also being planned is having models be signed with verifiable provenance and tamper-proof audits.

Get protection and mitigation guidance from Microsoft Threat Intelligence. (opens in new tab) 

Here is what we suggest as a starting point:

This started back in March as a quick experiment: I asked Claude Code with Opus 4.5 to backdoor a model by hardwiring a few activations without training. And it did. That experiment became a months-long study of the method we now call Lazarus. Here is what we learned:

  • Agents offer a large attack surface. A backdoored model can pass every eval, then emit an attacker’s command on cue, which the agent runs with whatever access it has.
  • Dormant neurons can be turned into trigger detectors. Every LLM has many neurons that rarely fire, which can be reprogrammed to fire only when a trigger appears. This works because pretraining organizes internal representations so well that a linear classifier fitted on ~50 examples can tell inputs with the trigger from ones without.
  • One reprogrammed neuron can inject one token. Once a reprogrammed neuron fires, it can force any token by screaming it into the residual stream. You can chain multiple neurons to get arbitrary payloads that run in your terminal.
  • It needs inference only compute. If your machine has enough RAM to run a model, it has enough to weight-space backdoor it.
  • This is not a case against open weights. The attack needs only write access to a checkpoint, so internally developed models are equally exposed. A compromised account, pipeline, or storage can be sufficient. What matters is weight integrity and provenance.
  • Weights should be audited like code. Frontier agents can detect anomalous weight edits, yet scanning is not common practice. That should change.
  • [!!!] Claude Code with Opus 4.5 discovered most of this autonomously

This is a simplified depiction of how Lazarus works.
